# Reference Models: Spike and Sail

## Concepts

### Architectural simulation and its purpose

This chapter summarizes the discussion of Spike and Sail in *RISC-V System-on-Chip Design* [@harrisRiscvSoc], principally Sections 3.3 and 3.5, with the testing context from Section 3.7 and the comparison methodology from Section 5.6. The worked program is an original exercise for this book.

An instruction-set simulator (ISS) executes a program according to the architectural meaning of its instructions. It maintains the program counter, registers, memory, privilege state, and relevant control and status registers (CSRs). For an addition, it computes the architecturally visible result; for a branch, it selects the next instruction address. This makes an ISS useful before hardware exists and as a reference when checking an implementation.

Architectural behavior and microarchitectural behavior answer different questions. An ISS can tell us what an instruction should write, but it does not normally tell us how many clock cycles a particular pipeline needs, which forwarding path is used, or whether a cache misses. Spike and the Sail simulator discussed in the book are functional models, not cycle-accurate implementations of Wally. A matching result therefore supports functional correctness, while timing, throughput, and physical implementation require other measurements.

A reference model is also not an infallible oracle. Its revision, configuration, assumptions, and supported specification versions matter. When a disagreement appears, first establish whether the models are executing the same program in the same architectural environment. Only then classify it as an RTL defect, a reference-model issue, or a legal implementation difference.

### Spike: a practical functional model

Spike is an open-source RISC-V ISS originally developed at Berkeley. It can model one or more harts, where a hart is an independently executing architectural context. The book uses a single hart for introductory exercises, selecting it as hart 0 in debugger commands. Spike executes machine-code instructions and offers an interactive monitor for inspecting registers, memory, and control flow.

The book explains that Spike historically served as the principal RISC-V reference model, while Sail supplies the formal executable reference in the workflow it describes. Spike remains convenient for learning assembly and debugging small programs. Its command-line monitor allows a student to stop at a specific program counter, inspect an intermediate result, and continue without building a SystemVerilog testbench.

Spike belongs beside the compiler, assembler, linker, and binary inspection tools. It is not itself a compiler: GCC produces the RISC-V executable, and Spike consumes it. An executable that runs on the host computer is not interchangeable with a RISC-V executable, even when both use the ELF container format.

### Sail: language, specification, and simulator

The name Sail refers to three related things. First, Sail is a language for specifying instruction-set behavior. Second, the RISC-V Sail model describes the ISA in that language. Third, an executable simulator is generated from that description and is commonly called the Sail simulator. The supplied edition names this executable `sail_riscv_sim`, while some older environments provide separate `riscv_sim_RV32` and `riscv_sim_RV64` binaries.

The distinction is important: running a RISC-V executable through the Sail simulator does not mean writing a program in Sail. The test program remains assembly or C compiled into RISC-V instructions. Sail defines the operations those instructions perform.

Section 3.5 presents Sail as a precise, executable architectural specification that resolves ambiguities in prose descriptions in the book's reference flow. An instruction definition specifies operand interpretation, extension, arithmetic or logical operation, destination update, and completion. For example, an immediate arithmetic instruction must specify how its immediate is sign-extended and whether a comparison is signed or unsigned. Similar-looking instructions can differ in exactly these details.

The specification can generate an emulator and definitions used by theorem provers. Sharing a semantic source reduces duplication between documentation and executable behavior. It does not automatically prove a complex processor correct: the implementation, environment, and proof obligations still have to be related to that specification.

### ELF, ISA, and ABI must agree

The book builds executable files using the GNU RISC-V cross-toolchain. A prefix such as `riscv64-unknown-elf-` identifies a toolchain target, not necessarily the width of every program it can produce. A suitable multilib installation can support both RV32 and RV64. Select the intended instruction set with `-march` and calling convention with `-mabi`.

The ISA defines instructions and architectural state. The ABI additionally defines data sizes and calling conventions: argument/result registers, preserved registers, stack conventions, and executable organization. For example, RV64 code can use the integer `lp64` ABI, while floating-point calling conventions require appropriate extensions and ABI selection. Simulator configuration must support the instructions actually emitted, including compressed instructions or CSR accesses introduced by the toolchain.

ELF holds entry-point information, loadable segments, code/data sections, and symbols. The linker places those objects into an address map and resolves references. A bare-metal image needs a valid entry point and any required startup state; a simulator does not magically initialize a software stack or provide the C library's services. Use `readelf` to inspect metadata and `objdump -d` to inspect instructions. Disassembling all sections with `-D` can misleadingly interpret ordinary data as instructions.

### Completion and signatures

Small bare-metal programs often end in a loop so that execution cannot fall into unrelated memory. That loop is a safe stopping location for manual debugging, but an automated test needs a completion mechanism. The book uses the host-target interface (HTIF), with an aligned, eight-byte object named `tohost`. Writing 1 signals successful completion in this convention; writing 3 reports failure.

HTIF is a test-environment convention, not an instruction in the RISC-V ISA or an automatic peripheral of every SoC. The ELF symbol table lets the simulator locate the mailbox. A warning about missing `tohost`/`fromhost` symbols can be tolerable for a deliberately interactive exercise, but it is a problem when a batch test depends on that mailbox to finish. Hosted programs may instead use a proxy kernel or another runtime to supply services.

A signature is a designated memory region containing test results. Labels `begin_signature` and `end_signature` delimit it. The simulator exports that region, making it possible to compare results independently of debugger output. A completion flag and a correct signature are different evidence: a program may reach its success exit without recording all relevant architectural effects.

### Counters and performance claims

The book's `sumtest` exercise sums integers from 1 through 4, writes the result and a retired-instruction count into a signature, and signals completion through HTIF. For the particular assembly listing and measurement boundaries shown there, the results are 10 and 29, hexadecimal `0A` and `1D`. Those counts depend on the exact instruction sequence, including the call and counter-reading boundary; they are not universal values for every implementation of a summation.

The `instret` CSR counts retired instructions, while `cycle` represents a cycle counter. The book warns that Spike advances these in a simplified functional execution model. A real processor may stall, flush instructions, or spend additional cycles on memory and arithmetic. An ISS instruction count can help explain algorithmic work, but it cannot establish Wally's CPI or the benefit of a cache configuration.

The book also reports that the Sail model was substantially slower than Spike in its test-generation environment. Treat that as context for choosing interactive versus reference workloads, not a portable benchmark. Host machine, model version, tracing, extensions, and workload all affect runtime.

### From reference execution to differential verification

The examples here run architectural models and stop short of wiring a retirement comparator into the Wally testbench. That is the natural next step, and follow @sec-verification-methodology: match ISA/privilege/memory settings, align committed instructions and trap events, and compare register/CSR/memory effects under a documented nondeterminism policy. Pipeline cycles and reference-model steps need not coincide. Counter, device and interrupt differences require explicit synchronization or narrowly justified exclusions. Keep signature tests as fast checks while stating which unrecorded intermediate effects they can miss.


## Implementation

### Configure equivalent environments

Before comparing models, record XLEN, ISA extensions, privilege support, memory map, entry point, hart count, CSR behavior, and external inputs. Defaults are convenient for a first demonstration but unsuitable as an undocumented reference configuration. The same instruction may trap in one configuration and execute normally in another.

The supplied edition describes a JSON configuration for `sail_riscv_sim`. Its default configuration can be printed and used as a starting point. The current [Sail RISC-V documentation](https://github.com/riscv/sail-riscv) also describes JSON configuration and the generated simulator. A Wally configuration file must correspond to the checked-out model's schema; copying a file across incompatible releases can introduce errors.

For Spike, `--isa` selects the architectural instruction set. For Sail, use the installed binary's help and configuration mechanism. A model that supports a superset of the exercise's instructions is adequate for demonstrating results, but a processor conformance experiment must also verify that unsupported instructions are rejected.

### Reading an instruction trace

A useful trace associates each executed instruction with its PC, encoding, privilege context, and architectural updates. Sail's trace in Section 3.5 displays integer-register writes, CSR operations, and memory transactions. The summation trace connects the loaded input, loop iterations, returned result, signature stores, and HTIF completion.

Compare traces at architectural boundaries. Wally may have several instructions in flight and speculative instructions that are later discarded. A pipeline cycle therefore cannot be matched against one ISS step. For a retired instruction, identify its PC, destination register/value, memory effect, and any trap. If the final signature differs, find the first divergent instruction rather than starting from the final incorrect value.

Interrupts and peripheral inputs need special treatment. A lockstep reference must receive equivalent events and read values; otherwise the instruction streams diverge for environmental reasons. Section 5.6 presents this principle without claiming that a standalone Spike or Sail command automatically provides a Wally lockstep integration.

### Architectural tests and their limits

Section 3.7 describes the book's RISCOF workflow: select tests compatible with a declared ISA, compile them, run reference models, and compare signatures. The resulting ELF, disassembly, and memory image can support the RTL testbench. Configuration is part of the experiment, not merely a build convenience.

The book distinguishes architectural tests from additional Wally tests for privilege, memory management, and peripherals. In its described setup, not every peripheral behavior is represented by Sail, so some expected outputs are supplied separately. When expected data is written by hand, have someone review it independently, because the reference model cannot catch a wrong prediction that it never computed.

A finite suite that passes shows the tested behavior is right, and complete ISA correctness is a larger claim. A signature may omit important flags, traps or side effects. Combine instruction tests, retirement-state comparison, assertions, and system scenarios. A coverage plan should say which requirements each technique observes and which remain untested.

## Hands-on Experiments

### Common program and build

Download the files and save them together in a working directory:

- [check.S](../../examples/reference-models/check.S): assembly test program.
- [link.ld](../../examples/reference-models/link.ld): linker script.
- [expected.signature](../../examples/reference-models/expected.signature): expected results.

Keep the exact filenames. If your browser displays a file as text, use **Save link as**. For a standalone download, run the build and simulation commands from your working directory instead of changing to the repository's example directory.

The files in `examples/reference-models/` implement an original RV64I test shared by both examples. It performs three checks: 28 + 9 = 37; the sum of integers 1 through 6 = 21; and a signed comparison of -1 with 1 = true. Results are stored as three 64-bit signature words. Explicit checks select HTIF success or failure.

The program avoids stack accesses, libraries, CSR counters, and compressed instructions. Its linker script places code at `0x80000000`, provides aligned mailbox/data regions, and selects `_start`. This isolates basic arithmetic, branches, signed comparison, loads of addresses, and stores from more complex runtime requirements.

From the repository root, in Linux or a suitable WSL/container environment:

```sh
cd examples/reference-models
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -march=rv64i -mabi=lp64 \
  -nostdlib -nostartfiles -mcmodel=medany -Wl,--no-relax \
  -T link.ld -o check.elf check.S
riscv64-unknown-elf-readelf -h check.elf
riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d check.elf > check.dump
```

Check ELF64, RISC-V machine type, and entry point `0x80000000`. The compiler flags deliberately exclude automatic startup and libraries; the assembly supplies its own entry and termination. Linker relaxation is disabled to make address construction easier to inspect.

The expected numeric signature, supplied in `expected.signature`, is:

```text
0000000000000025
0000000000000015
0000000000000001
```

These are hexadecimal words: `25` means decimal 37 and `15` means decimal 21. The third word is a Boolean result represented as an integer.

### Example 1: run and debug with Spike

[Core option · P2 · C2 build / C1 run](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-spike-example .learning-activity}

**Checked recipe:** RV64I signature run with Spike 1.1.1-dev and the stated toolchain. Use the example working directory; stop on a failed run rather than accepting an older signature.

With Spike available in `PATH`, run the batch test and compare its signature:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -f -- spike.sig
timeout 20s spike --isa=rv64i \
  +signature=spike.sig +signature-granularity=8 check.elf
diff -i expected.signature spike.sig
```

Both commands should return zero; silent `diff` means agreement. The timeout bounds an accidentally nonterminating test and returns nonzero on expiry. After a simulation failure, a stale signature from a previous run is not evidence, so make sure the file is fresh.

For an interactive run:

```sh
spike --isa=rv64i -d check.elf
```

At the monitor, type `help`, then press Enter to step. The initial trace can include simulator startup instructions before reaching the ELF entry point. To inspect architectural registers, use:

```text
until reg 0 a1 15
reg 0 a0
reg 0 a1
reg 0 a2
q
```

The `until` condition stops when the loop's result reaches hexadecimal 15. At that point `a0` should hold 25; `a2` is not yet guaranteed to contain its final comparison result, so step further to the comparison before checking it. A stop condition must actually be reached before HTIF completion. Debugger `reg` is a monitor command, unrelated to an HDL declaration. See the [Spike project documentation](https://github.com/riscv-software-src/riscv-isa-sim) for current monitor syntax.

### Example 2: run and trace with Sail

[Advanced · C2 build / C1 run](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-sail-example .learning-activity}

**Adaptation template:** the modern `sail_riscv_sim` command was not executed in the recorded environment. The older RV64 executable recipe below was checked; use only the CLI/options supported by the selected installation.

For the `sail_riscv_sim` interface used in the supplied edition, inspect help and save its default configuration before running:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -f -- sail.sig
sail_riscv_sim --help
sail_riscv_sim --print-default-config > sail-default.json
timeout 20s sail_riscv_sim --config sail-default.json \
  --test-signature sail.sig --signature-granularity 8 \
  --trace-all check.elf > sail.log 2>&1
diff -i expected.signature sail.sig
```

Use an RV64 configuration supporting the program and its HTIF test environment. This demonstration accepts the default extension superset; matching Wally strictly requires editing the configuration to the intended core. Check the installed release's help for trace/signature options, since those interfaces vary.

Read `sail.log` around the arithmetic, loop exit, signature stores, and completion. The stored values should match the three expected words above. Generating a signature is not enough: check the process result and compare the contents.

An older Sail installation with a separate RV64 executable uses this equivalent command:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -f -- sail.sig
timeout 20s riscv_sim_RV64 --no-trace \
  --test-signature sail.sig --signature-granularity 8 check.elf
diff -i expected.signature sail.sig
diff -i spike.sig sail.sig
```

The shared program was compiled and run successfully using Spike 1.1.1-dev and this older Sail executable in the local Wally toolchain container. Both produced the expected three-word signature. The newer `sail_riscv_sim` command documents the PDF's workflow and was not executed in that container.

Signature formatting matters: different granularities may split or reverse groups within a wider word. Use matching eight-byte granularity here. For other tools, compare decoded values using the documented byte ordering; rearranging lines until the text matches hides real differences.

### Diagnose and extend the experiment

[Advanced · C1 local / C2 system](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-isa-differential .learning-activity}

If execution traps before a signature store, inspect the instruction encoding and enabled extensions. If execution never completes, check the loop, entry point, mailbox symbols, and mapped addresses. If models disagree only on counters or peripheral state, check environmental assumptions before changing arithmetic RTL.

Change one expected sum or comparison deliberately and confirm that the program signals failure. Then add boundary cases such as unsigned wraparound and signed-versus-unsigned comparisons, expanding signature storage accordingly. Keep the same ELF for both models.

Finally, run the program on a configured RTL core and compare the defined signature. Preserve the executable, disassembly, configuration, model revisions, exit statuses, and logs. This turns a pair of simulator demonstrations into a reproducible architectural check while leaving pipeline timing and physical implementation to their appropriate verification flows.

## Key ideas {#review-spike-sail-ideas .unnumbered .unlisted}

- An ISA reference checks architectural behavior; RTL cycle timing is a different question.
- Model version, ISA configuration and execution environment must agree.

## What you should now be able to explain {#review-spike-sail-explain .unnumbered .unlisted}

Explain the signature comparison boundary and what a reference-model pass cannot establish about caches, timing or FPGA behavior.

## Common mistakes {#review-spike-sail-mistakes .unnumbered .unlisted}

Two comparisons look meaningful and are not. Results from incompatible ISA or platform configurations cannot be set side by side. And the wall-clock time of an instruction-set simulator reflects the host machine, so it is not the performance of the target processor.

## Try it yourself {#review-spike-sail-try .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Preparation · C0](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-spike-sail-review .learning-activity}

Follow the supplied signature example from ELF loading to final comparison. Name the first architectural observation you would compare with RTL.

## Where this appears in Wally {#review-spike-sail-wally .unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.callout-note title="Wally Connection" icon=false}
Use [config/rv32gc/config.vh](https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/cvw/blob/3b30ba6b6519bd2c26c1437e6d61f632a35cef6c/config/rv32gc/config.vh) to select matching ISA features and [src/wally/wallypipelinedcore.sv](https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/cvw/blob/3b30ba6b6519bd2c26c1437e6d61f632a35cef6c/src/wally/wallypipelinedcore.sv) to locate the RTL core boundary. Reference agreement does not verify every internal event.
:::
